title: "Extrahepatic Portal Venous Obstruction (EHPVO)"

  revealjs:

## EHPVO at a Glance

- A **leading cause of non-cirrhotic portal hypertension** in developing countries
- Especially affects **children and adolescents**
- Characterized by **chronic extrahepatic portal vein thrombosis** with **cavernomatous transformation**
- Leads to:
  - Recurrent variceal bleeding
  - Hypersplenism
  - Portal biliopathy
- Hepatic parenchymal function is **generally preserved** — distinguishing it from cirrhosis

## Why Revisit EHPVO Now?

- The therapeutic landscape has **evolved significantly** in recent years
- Transformative advances over the past two decades in:
  - Diagnostic imaging
  - **Endovascular recanalization**
  - **Physiologic shunt surgery** (e.g., meso-Rex bypass)
- This review provides an **updated clinical framework** emphasizing:
  - Modern endovascular recanalization strategies
  - Evolving concepts in portal cavernoma cholangiopathy (PCC)
  - Pediatric versus adult management priorities
  - Emerging technologies — AI-assisted vascular planning, hybrid approaches

## Section: Epidemiology & Etiology {.title-slide}

## Epidemiology: Global Perspective

- Accounts for **15–30%** of portal hypertension cases in India and other tropical regions
- In Western countries, contribution **rarely exceeds 10%**
- Recent Indian hospital-based registries:
  - EHPVO prevalence among portal hypertension referrals ≈ **35%**
- Ongoing **public health relevance** in tropical regions
- Male preponderance in Indian series: **M:F ≈ 2:1** (less pronounced in Western cohorts)

## Epidemiology: Tropical vs Western Settings

| Feature | Tropical regions (South / South-east Asia) | Western countries |
|---|---|---|
| Typical age at diagnosis | **Childhood and adolescence** | Usually **adults** |
| Frequency | Common; major cause of non-cirrhotic portal hypertension | Uncommon (<10% of portal hypertension) |
| Typical etiology | Neonatal / childhood insults | Prothrombotic disorders, incidental adult detection |
| Disease burden | Lifelong: recurrent GI bleeding, growth retardation, portal biliopathy | Often longstanding, unrecognized childhood disease |

## Age at Presentation

- **Children:**
  - Mean age at presentation: **6–10 years**
  - Typically follows an initial episode of **variceal bleeding**
- **Adults:**
  - Diagnosis is often **incidental**
  - During evaluation for **splenomegaly or cytopenias**
  - Reflects longstanding, unrecognized childhood disease

## Etiology: Pediatric EHPVO

Predominant factors in children:

- **Neonatal sepsis**
- **Umbilical vein catheterization**
- **Omphalitis**
- **Dehydration**
- **Intra-abdominal infection**

::: {.callout-warning}
Socioeconomic and environmental factors in tropical settings contribute substantially: unhygienic cord care, limited access to neonatal intensive care, and high infectious burden.
:::

## Etiology: Adult EHPVO

Acquired **prothrombotic states** are prominent in adults:

- Myeloproliferative disorders (MPN)
- Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS)
- Protein C / S deficiency
- Factor V Leiden mutation
- Oral contraceptive use

Despite comprehensive evaluation, **30–40% of EHPVO cases remain idiopathic**.

## Table 1: Etiologic Spectrum of EHPVO in Tropical Countries

:::{.smaller}
| Category | Specific causes / examples | Relative frequency (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Neonatal insults | Sepsis, omphalitis, umbilical vein catheterization | **30–40** |
| Infections (childhood) | Intra-abdominal infection, dehydration | 10–15 |
| Prothrombotic disorders | Protein C/S deficiency, factor V Leiden, APS, MPN | 20–25 |
| Post-surgical / iatrogenic | Abdominal surgery, trauma | 5–10 |
| Idiopathic | No identifiable factor | **20–40** |
:::

::: {.callout-note}
Neonatal insults dominate in children; prothrombotic disorders are relatively more important in adults.
:::

## Idiopathic EHPVO & Tropical Contributors

- Up to **30–40%** of cases remain **idiopathic** even after comprehensive evaluation
- Tropical setting adds specific risks:
  - Unhygienic cord care
  - Limited access to neonatal intensive care
  - High infectious burden
- These factors explain the higher disease frequency in developing regions

## EHPVO vs Chronic Portal Vein Thrombosis

- EHPVO is often equated with chronic PVT, but important differences exist:

| Dimension | EHPVO (tropical) | Chronic PVT (Western) |
|---|---|---|
| Typical patient | Children, after neonatal/childhood insults | Adults with prothrombotic disorders or malignancy |
| Typical features | Growth failure, massive splenomegaly, portal biliopathy | Variable; often related to underlying disease |
| Therapeutic focus | **Physiologic shunt surgery (meso-Rex shunt)** | Treat underlying liver disease, anticoagulation, TIPS or liver transplantation (if cirrhosis) |

## Section: Pathophysiology {.title-slide}

## Pathophysiology: The Initiating Event

1. **Acute thrombotic obstruction** of the main portal vein or its tributaries
2. Over weeks: **thrombus organization and fibrosis**
3. Result: **permanent occlusion** of the portal vein
4. Obstruction may extend to the **splenic vein** or **superior mesenteric vein**

## Portal Cavernoma Formation

- To maintain **hepatopetal flow**, numerous small **periportal collaterals** develop
- These collaterals are collectively termed the **portal cavernoma**
- The cavernoma reroutes mesenteric venous blood toward the liver
- **Collateralization preserves hepatic function** — but at a cost:
  - Elevated splanchnic pressure
  - Splenomegaly and hypersplenism
  - Gastroesophageal varices

## Hemodynamic State

- EHPVO induces a unique hemodynamic state:
  - **Presinusoidal hypertension**
  - **Preserved sinusoidal architecture**
- The **hepatic artery enlarges** compensatorily to sustain parenchymal perfusion
- Preserved liver architecture underlies the excellent hepatic reserve seen in EHPVO

## Consequences of Portal Hypertension

- **Spleen:** congested and hyperfunctional
  - Thrombocytopenia and anemia (hypersplenism)
  - Low-grade systemic inflammation and impaired immunity may occur
- **Varices:** gastroesophageal varices → recurrent upper GI bleeding
- **Biliary tree:** portal biliopathy (see later)
- **Growth:** retardation in children

## Growth Retardation in Children

Longstanding elevated portal pressure contributes to growth retardation through:

- Reduced nutrient absorption
- Hypersplenism-related cytopenias
- Impaired **insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1)** signaling

::: {.callout-important}
Growth failure is a hallmark of longstanding pediatric EHPVO — and a key indication for definitive (physiologic) shunt surgery.
:::

## Pathogenesis of Portal Biliopathy

Portal biliopathy arises from two mechanisms:

1. **Extrinsic compression** of the bile duct by peribiliary collaterals
2. **Ischemic cholangiopathy** due to loss of the peribiliary vascular plexus

Longstanding disease → biliary complications collectively known as **portal biliopathy** or **portal cavernoma cholangiopathy (PCC)**.

## Figure 1: Pathogenesis and Clinical Features of EHPVO

:::{.smaller}
```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[Acute thrombotic obstruction of PV / tributaries] --> B[Thrombus organization & fibrosis]
    B --> C[Chronic PV occlusion]
    C --> D[Periportal collaterals: PORTAL CAVERNOMA]
    D --> E[Hepatopetal flow maintained - hepatic function preserved]
    D --> F[Elevated splanchnic pressure - presinusoidal portal hypertension]
    F --> G[Gastroesophageal varices → recurrent bleeding]
    F --> H[Congestive splenomegaly → hypersplenism]
    F --> I[Growth retardation in children]
    D --> J[Peribiliary collaterals + ischemic cholangiopathy]
    J --> K[Portal biliopathy / PCC]
    C --> L[Hepatic artery compensatory enlargement]
```
:::

## Section: Natural History & Diagnosis {.title-slide}

## Natural History: Typical Presentation

Patients typically present with:

- **Upper gastrointestinal bleeding** from varices
- **Massive splenomegaly**
- **Hypersplenism**
- Liver function tests often **normal or mildly deranged**
- Some adults present with **jaundice or recurrent cholangitis** due to PCC
- In the older age group:
  - Parenchymal extinction may occur
  - May manifest as **ascites** and **hepatic encephalopathy**

## Natural History: Survival & Variceal Development

- **5-year survival:** ≈ **96%**
- Probability of variceal development:
  - **1-year:** 2%
  - **5-year:** 22%

::: {.callout-note}
EHPVO carries an excellent survival outlook, but imposes a lifelong burden of recurrent bleeding, hypersplenism, and potential biliary complications.
:::

## Laboratory Profile

- **Pancytopenia** (from hypersplenism)
- **Normal albumin**
- **Normal prothrombin time**
- Liver enzymes: normal or mildly deranged
- **Thrombophilia screening recommended:**
  - Particularly in **adults**
  - And in **idiopathic cases**

## First-Line Imaging: Color Doppler Ultrasonography

- First-line diagnostic test
- Demonstrates:
  - **Absence of normal portal flow**
  - **Multiple serpiginous collaterals** (portal cavernoma)
- Non-invasive, widely available, and suitable for screening and follow-up

## Cross-Sectional & Advanced Imaging

- **Contrast-enhanced CT and MR portography:**
  - Map venous anatomy
  - Aid planning for shunt surgery or recanalization
- **MRCP:** evaluates biliary abnormalities (PCC)
- **Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS):**
  - Differentiates vascular from non-vascular compression
  - Assesses pericholedochal collaterals
- **Advanced tools:**
  - Four-dimensional (4D) flow MRI
  - Contrast-enhanced ultrasound
  - Can **quantify portal hemodynamics**

## Figure 2: MRI Findings in EHPVO

Post-contrast coronal MRI demonstrates the classic constellation:

- **Portal cavernoma** — serpiginous periportal collaterals
- **Pericholecystic collaterals**
- **Dilated biliary radicles** (biliary involvement / PCC)
- **Splenomegaly** with **Gamma-Gandy bodies** (siderotic nodules from congestive splenopathy)

::: {.callout-note}
*Figure 2 of the article: post-contrast coronal MRI showing portal cavernoma, pericholecystic collaterals with dilated biliary radicles, and splenomegaly with Gamma-Gandy bodies.*
:::

## Figure 3: MRCP Findings in Portal Cavernoma Cholangiopathy

- **Coronal 3D MRCP** in a patient with EHPVO shows:
  - **Non-visualization of the mid common bile duct (CBD)**
  - Due to a **dominant biliary stricture**

::: {.callout-note}
MRCP is the investigation of choice for mapping biliary involvement when cholestasis is suspected; EUS complements it by identifying pericholedochal vessels before intervention.
:::

## Differential Diagnosis

Main differentials of EHPVO:

1. **Non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis (NCPF)**
2. **Budd-Chiari syndrome**
3. **Cirrhosis with chronic PVT**

Distinguishing pointers:

- **Preservation of liver architecture** favors EHPVO
- **Absence of hepatic vein obstruction** argues against Budd-Chiari
- Liver biopsy is **not routine** — reserved for when cirrhosis is a differential

## Table 2: EHPVO vs NCPF vs Cirrhosis — Clinical Features

:::{.smaller}
| Feature | EHPVO | NCPF | Cirrhosis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Etiology | Portal vein thrombosis (neonatal sepsis, catheter, thrombophilia) | Obliterative portal venopathy, idiopathic | Chronic liver injury (viral, alcohol, MASH) |
| Liver size & texture | Normal | Normal / slightly coarse | Shrunken, nodular |
| Splenomegaly | **Massive** | Moderate | Moderate |
| Variceal bleeding | **Very common, early** | Common | Common, late |
| Ascites | Rare, transient | Occasional | Frequent, persistent |
:::

## Table 2 (contd.): Investigations & Outcomes

:::{.smaller}
| Feature | EHPVO | NCPF | Cirrhosis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Liver function tests | Normal | Normal / mild ↑ alkaline phosphatase | Abnormal |
| Portal vein patency | **Occluded / cavernomatous** | Patent | Often patent |
| Hepatic veins | Patent | Patent | Patent / altered with advanced disease |
| Biliary changes | **Portal biliopathy** | None | Secondary to cirrhosis |
| Response to shunt surgery | Excellent | Variable | Risk of encephalopathy |
| Prognosis | **Excellent** | Good | Guarded |
:::

## Liver Biopsy in EHPVO

- **Not done routinely**
- Indicated when **cirrhosis is a differential diagnosis**
- Common biopsy findings:

| Finding | Frequency |
|---|---|
| Portal vein dilatation | 70% |
| Periportal aberrant vascular channels | 46% |
| Portal vein thickening | 28% |
| Portal vein narrowing | 10% |
| Remnant portal triads | 2% |
| Portal vein thrombosis | 1% |

- Fibrosis stage: predominantly **Ishak stage 1 to Ishak stage 3**

## A Practical Diagnostic Algorithm

1. **Confirm cavernoma** on Color Doppler ultrasonography
2. **Map vascular anatomy** with CT / MR portography
3. **Evaluate the biliary tract** with MRCP when cholestasis is suspected
4. **Thrombophilia workup** in adults or those with recurrent disease
5. Liver biopsy only if cirrhosis is in the differential

## Section: Management {.title-slide}

## Principles of Management

Management aims to:

- **Control bleeding**
- **Prevent rebleeding**
- **Decompress portal pressure**
- Address **hypersplenism, growth failure, and portal biliopathy**

::: {.callout-important}
Restoration of **physiologic portal flow** is emphasized whenever feasible.
:::

## Treatment Armamentarium

- Endoscopic therapy
- Surgical shunts
- **Meso-Rex bypass (MRS)**
- Endovascular recanalization
- Hybrid approaches
- Rarely: liver transplantation

Treatment selection depends on: **age, vascular anatomy, complications, and institutional expertise.**

## Strength of Evidence by Modality

- **Surgical shunts** (especially physiologic shunts like meso-Rex in children):
  - Strongest long-term outcome data
  - Durable patency, excellent bleeding control, growth improvement
- **Endovascular recanalization:**
  - Emerging cohort studies and single-center experiences
  - High technical success; encouraging mid-term patency
- **Endoscopic therapy:**
  - Essential for acute bleeding control and short-term management
  - Generally **bridging**, not definitive
- Direct comparisons limited by heterogeneity, follow-up duration, and rapidly evolving techniques

## Table 3: Comparative Outcomes — Efficacy

:::{.smaller}
| Parameter | Endoscopic therapy | Surgical shunts (PSRS / MRS / DSRS) | Endovascular / hybrid |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary goal | Variceal control | Definitive portal decompression | Physiologic / anatomic restoration |
| Rebleeding (%) | 30–40 | **<10** | 10–20 |
| Patency (5-year) | – | 85–90% | 70–80% |
| Effect on hypersplenism | None | Marked improvement | Moderate improvement |
| Growth recovery (children) | No | **>80%** | Variable |
:::

## Table 3 (contd.): Practical Considerations

:::{.smaller}
| Parameter | Endoscopic therapy | Surgical shunts | Endovascular / hybrid |
|---|---|---|---|
| Portal biliopathy relief | Minimal | 70–80% | ≈70% |
| Hepatic encephalopathy risk | Nil | Low (physiologic) / higher (non-physiologic) | Low |
| Hospital stay | Short | Moderate | Short |
| Technical demand | Low | High (surgery) | High |
| Durability | Temporary | Long term | Intermediate |
| Preferred setting | Acute bleed control | Definitive in children / fit adults | Adults or high surgical risk |
:::

## Management of Acute Variceal Bleeding

Managed **similarly to cirrhosis**:

- Resuscitation
- Vasoactive agents: **terlipressin or octreotide**
- Prophylactic antibiotics
- **Endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL)** — first-line for hemostasis
- Uncontrolled or recurrent bleeding:
  - Emergency **surgical** or **endovascular decompression**

## Secondary Prophylaxis

- **Serial EVL every 2–4 weeks** until variceal eradication
- Then **6-monthly surveillance** endoscopy
- **Non-selective beta-blockers** may be added
- Definitive therapy considered for:
  - Recurrent bleeding
  - Severe hypersplenism
  - Impaired growth
  - Symptomatic portal biliopathy

## Indications for Definitive Therapy

Definitive therapy = **physiologic shunt surgery** or **portal vein recanalization**

Consider in patients with:

1. Recurrent bleeding despite endoscopic therapy
2. Severe hypersplenism
3. Impaired growth (children)
4. Symptomatic portal biliopathy

## Portal Cavernoma Cholangiopathy: Classification

First, categorize patients into:

- **Asymptomatic (radiologic) PCC:**
  - Isolated radiologic abnormalities
  - Normal or minimally elevated liver enzymes
  - No cholangitis
  - → **Observation alone** with periodic follow-up
- **Clinically significant PCC:**
  - Jaundice, biliary pain, cholangitis, or dominant biliary strictures
  - → **Stepwise therapeutic approach**

## Management of PCC: Stepwise Approach

1. **ERCP-guided interventions:**
   - Biliary stenting, stone extraction, balloon dilatation, nasobiliary drainage
2. **Definitive portal decompression** (surgical shunting or endovascular PV recanalization):
   - For persistent symptoms, recurrent cholangitis, or severe biliary obstruction
3. **Second-stage biliary bypass** (Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy):
   - Minority with residual obstruction despite decompression

## UDCA in PCC: What Is the Evidence?

- Role of pharmacotherapy in PCC is **not clearly defined**
- No extensive study has assessed **ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA)** for treatment or prophylaxis
- Some studies (Condat, Perlemuter, Llop) reported symptom disappearance and liver-test improvement
- But other studies showed equally good results with endoscopic management **without** UDCA
- No study has compared **ERCP alone vs ERCP + UDCA**
- **Routine UDCA use cannot be recommended** — may be used case-by-case

## Endoscopic Management of PCC

Indications: biliary strictures, CBD stones, cholangitis, or when shunt surgery is not feasible

- **CBD stones:** Dormia baskets and/or balloon catheters
- Large stones: mechanical / laser lithotripsy
- **Cholangitis:** endoscopic papillotomy with stenting ± nasobiliary drainage
- **Dominant CBD strictures with stones:** balloon dilatation followed by stone removal
- **EUS** used with ERCP to identify perforators and subepithelial biliary vessels → safer drainage
- **Self-expanding fully covered metallic stents** increasingly used, especially with hemobilia

## Surgical Portal Decompression in PCC

- Goal: decompress the portal vasculature and reduce pressure in collaterals
  - Relieves biliary obstruction, variceal hemorrhage, hypersplenism
- Non-selective portosystemic shunts commonly created:
  - **Proximal splenorenal shunt (PSRS)**
  - **Mesocaval shunt**
- Less common: side-to-side splenorenal, meso-gonadal vein, meso-renal, porta-varix to vena cava shunts
- In most patients, a portosystemic shunt or Rex shunt **regresses pericholedochal collaterals** and relieves symptoms
- Non-responders / partial responders → **Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy**

## The Meso-Rex Shunt: Physiologic Restoration

- Shunt between the **mesenteric vein** and the **left portal vein** (Rex recessus)
- Commonly created in **pediatric EHPVO**
- Restores **physiologic hepatopetal portal flow**
- Benefits:
  - Excellent, durable bleeding control
  - Marked improvement in hypersplenism
  - **Growth recovery in >80% of children**
  - Low encephalopathy risk

## What About Patients With No Shuntable Veins?

Interventional radiology plays a key role:

- **Portal vein recanalization**
- **TIPS** (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting)
- **Portal vein reconstruction** (recanalization + stenting ± TIPS)

Surgical fallback:

- **Splenectomy and devascularization**

## Figure 4: Rescue TIPS After Shunt Occlusion — A Case

:::{.smaller}
A patient with EHPVO, post-splenectomy and proximal splenorenal shunt (PSRS), presenting with **uncontrolled hematemesis after PSRS occlusion**:

- **(A) Coronal CT:** portal cavernoma with portal biliopathy; prominent left gastric vein and gastric varices
- **(B) Portovenogram:** portal cavernoma with **retrograde flow** into the left gastric vein and gastric varices
- **(C) Post-TIPS portovenogram:** **disappearance of flow** into the cavernoma and gastric varices, with **antegrade flow via TIPS**
:::

::: {.callout-note}
Illustrates endovascular rescue when surgical shunts fail or no shuntable veins remain.
:::

## Splenectomy and Devascularization

- Controls portal hypertension-related manifestations:
  - Variceal bleeding
  - Hypersplenism
- Also **reduces pressure in pericholedochal collaterals**
  - Thereby improving symptoms related to PCC
- Option for patients without shuntable veins or where other approaches are not feasible

## Liver Transplantation: A Rare Option

- Reserved for select patients with EHPVO and PCC
- Exercised when patients are **troubled more by PCC-related symptoms** than by portal hypertension symptoms
- Caveat:
  - Transplant **does not decompress the splanchnic bed**
  - Patients may continue to have hypersplenism and esophagogastric variceal symptoms

## Surgical vs Endovascular: Weighing the Evidence

Direct comparison is **problematic** because of:

- Differences in patient selection
- Variable follow-up duration
  - Surgical series: often 5–10-year outcomes
  - Endovascular series: typically 1–3 years
- Rapid evolution of endovascular techniques

Balanced view:

- **Surgical shunts:** excellent durability over decades; require major surgery and suitable anatomy
- **Endovascular approaches:** minimally invasive; shorter follow-up; potential need for reintervention
- Optimal approach depends on **individual anatomy, age, local expertise, and patient preferences**

## Endovascular Recanalization: Performance

- Access routes: **transhepatic, transsplenic, or transmesenteric**
- Combined with **angioplasty and stenting**
- **Technical success:** ≈ **80–90%**
- **5-year patency:** ≈ **70–80%** in selected anatomies
- **Hybrid open-endovascular approaches** show promise in complex or post-surgical cases

::: {.callout-warning}
Candidates are a select subset: favorable anatomy, absent cirrhosis, treated at high-volume centers. Generalizability to broader populations and resource-limited settings needs validation.
:::

## Figure 5: Algorithmic Approach to EHPVO Management

:::{.smaller}
```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[Suspected EHPVO: variceal bleed, splenomegaly, cytopenias] --> B[Color Doppler US: confirm portal cavernoma]
    B --> C[CT / MR portography: map vascular anatomy]
    C --> D{Clinical scenario?}
    D -->|Acute variceal bleed| E[Resuscitation + vasoactive drugs + antibiotics + EVL]
    E --> F[Secondary prophylaxis: serial EVL ± NSBB]
    D -->|Incidental / asymptomatic| G[Surveillance; assess complications]
    D -->|Cholestasis / cholangitis| H[MRCP ± EUS: evaluate PCC]
    H --> I[ERCP: stenting, stone extraction, dilatation]
    F --> J{Recurrent bleed / hypersplenism / growth failure / symptomatic PCC?}
    J -->|Yes| K[Definitive therapy]
    K --> L[Children: meso-Rex shunt when feasible]
    K --> M[Adults: PSRS / other portosystemic shunts]
    K --> N[Selected: endovascular recanalization ± TIPS]
    I --> O{Persistent severe obstruction?}
    O -->|Yes| P[Portal decompression; if residual → Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy]
```
:::

## Section: Pediatric vs Adult EHPVO {.title-slide}

## Pediatric vs Adult: Divergent Priorities

| Domain | Pediatric EHPVO | Adult EHPVO |
|---|---|---|
| Preferred shunt | **Physiologic shunting** (meso-Rex when feasible) | Portosystemic shunts or endovascular approaches |
| Critical goal | **Growth restoration** | Managing established portal biliopathy |
| Durability | Long-term patency essential | Balance of durability vs invasiveness |
| Safety concerns | Minimize radiation; avoid encephalopathy | Anticoagulation risks; fertility / pregnancy in women |

## Pediatric Management Priorities

- **Physiologic shunting preferred** — meso-Rex when feasible
- **Growth restoration is critical**
- **Long-term patency essential** (lifelong disease horizon)
- **Minimize radiation exposure**
- **Avoid hepatic encephalopathy**
- Surveillance: **growth monitoring** and developmental assessment

## Adult Management Priorities

- **Portosystemic shunts or endovascular approaches** more common than in children
- Managing **established portal biliopathy**
- Addressing **fertility / pregnancy concerns** in women
- **Balancing anticoagulation risks** (prothrombotic states common)
- Surveillance: **biliary surveillance** and endoscopic variceal follow-up

## Anticoagulation in EHPVO: Current Position

- **Limited role in chronic pediatric EHPVO**
- More commonly used in adults with **identified prothrombotic states**
- **No randomized trials** compare anticoagulation regimens specifically in EHPVO
- Most recommendations extrapolated from **cirrhotic PVT or Budd-Chiari syndrome** management
- **DOACs** increasingly used — but comparative effectiveness vs warfarin in EHPVO is limited

## Surveillance Strategy

**Children:**

- Growth monitoring
- Developmental assessment

**Adults:**

- Biliary surveillance (PCC increases with disease duration)
- Endoscopic variceal follow-up

## Section: Outcomes & Future Directions {.title-slide}

## Outcomes: Excellent With Systematic Care

- **10-year survival exceeds 90%** (5-year survival ≈ 96%)
- Rebleeding:
  - **<10%** after definitive shunt
  - vs **30–40%** with endoscopic therapy alone
- **Growth recovery in >80% of children** after meso-Rex shunt
- PCC incidence **increases with disease duration**
- Quality of life **improves substantially** after decompression
- Hepatic encephalopathy is **rare** — except with extensive non-physiologic shunts

## Interpreting Outcome Data Across Eras

- Outcome data must be interpreted in the context of **evolving therapeutic eras**:
  - **Earlier cohorts:** primarily surgical or endoscopic therapy
  - **Contemporary series:** increasingly incorporate endovascular and hybrid approaches
- Enabled by improved imaging and stent technology
- Long-term durability data for newer endovascular techniques are still maturing

## Emerging Directions: Endovascular Innovation

- **Newer covered stents** and **dual-access techniques** (transhepatic + transsplenic):
  - Technical success improved to **≈90%**
  - Multi-year patency achieved
- **Standardized anticoagulation pathways:**
  - Sequential low-molecular-weight heparin → **DOAC**
  - Enhance patency without excess bleeding

::: {.callout-warning}
Covered portal stents, dual-access recanalization, and AI-assisted planning currently have limited prospective outcome data — consider them **adjunctive rather than standard** approaches.
:::

## Emerging Directions: AI & Personalized Planning

- **AI-assisted vascular segmentation**
- **Three-dimensional (3D) printing**
- Applications:
  - Complex **meso-Rex** planning
  - **Hybrid** procedure planning
- May further refine future management pathways in multidisciplinary EHPVO care

## Transition Care: A Growing Need

- Pediatric survivors are increasingly entering adulthood
- Transition care must address:
  - **Fertility**
  - **Pregnancy** management
  - **Bone health**
- A growing need as long-term survival becomes the norm

## Conclusions

- EHPVO remains a **significant cause of non-cirrhotic portal hypertension** in tropical countries
- With systematic management it now carries an **excellent prognosis**
- Advances in imaging, physiologic shunting, endovascular recanalization, and hybrid interventions have **substantially expanded therapeutic options**
- Contemporary management emphasizes:
  - **Restoration of physiologic portal flow**
  - **Individualized treatment strategies**
  - **Multidisciplinary care**
- Emerging technologies (AI-assisted vascular planning) may refine future pathways — providing **new perspectives** for modern EHPVO care

## Key Takeaways

:::{.smaller}
1. EHPVO = chronic extrahepatic PV thrombosis + portal cavernoma; **preserved liver function**, presinusoidal portal hypertension
2. In tropical regions it is predominantly a **disease of children** (15–30% of portal hypertension; ≈35% of referrals in Indian registries)
3. Diagnosis: Doppler → CT/MR portography → MRCP (if cholestasis) → thrombophilia workup (adults/idiopathic)
4. Acute bleeding: treat like cirrhosis (vasoactive drugs + EVL); endoscopy is **bridging**, not definitive
5. **Meso-Rex shunt** is the pediatric gold standard — growth recovery in >80%
6. PCC: distinguish asymptomatic radiologic disease (observe) from clinically significant disease (ERCP → decompression → hepaticojejunostomy if needed); **routine UDCA not recommended**
7. Endovascular recanalization: 80–90% technical success, 70–80% 5-year patency in selected patients
8. 10-year survival **>90%** with definitive therapy; rebleeding <10%
:::
